How to use this book
Start with the three short “Start Here” lessons, even if you are unsure whether your website is already a PWA.
Then work through Chapters 1–38.
The Windows Toolkit Cookbook (Chapters 39–42) appears together just before the appendices so it is easy to find.
You can also jump to it whenever the Excel workbook or Doctor asks you to.
Read the story pictures and the three beginner pages.
Try one small task at a time.
You do not have to complete a whole chapter in one sitting.
For each action, compare the described result with what you see, not just with the illustration.
Keep passwords and secret files private; never paste them into the Excel notes.
Record PASS, WARN, FAIL, or Not Started in the workbook and add one plain-English sentence about the result.
If something looks different: The pictures are simulations of interfaces that can change.
Find the control with the same purpose, and record any confusing differences rather than guessing.

CHAPTER 37 · WINDOWS COOKBOOK
Maintain Your App After Release
Publishing is not the finish line.
This chapter explains simple habits for keeping the app working and safe.
Here is what to do
For each update record version, date, what changed, what devices were tested, and whether the store accepted it.
Recheck privacy and device behavior after meaningful changes.
Keep secure backups of the source, signing files, and versioned release artifacts.
Make a small test change, build a new version, and test it before store submission.
Monitor store reviews, crash reports, security updates, and privacy-policy changes.
Record each release date, version number, tester outcome, and store approval in the workbook.

Plan Google’s Required Closed Testing
Some Google Play accounts must complete a closed test before publishing.
We will check whether that rule applies to your account.
Here is what to do
For affected personal Google Play accounts, the published guidance has required at least 12 opted-in testers over 14 continuous days; confirm the current rule for your account.
Ask for genuine feedback, obtain consent, and track opt-in dates without publishing testers’ private details.
Complete this BEFORE Chapter 36 production submission.
Check whether your personal developer account was created after November 13, 2023 and falls under Google’s production-access testing requirement.
If applicable, invite at least 12 testers who opt in continuously for at least 14 days; additional account-specific requirements may apply.
Share the official testing invite link; ask testers to use the app and provide genuine feedback.
Do not buy fake enrollments or share credentials.
Track each tester’s opt-in and feedback without storing unnecessary personal data.
Check the live Play Console before applying for production access.

CHAPTER 40 · WINDOWS COOKBOOK
Repair Windows Tool Paths
Doctor may say that Windows cannot find a program even when the program is installed.
We will check that safely.
Here is what to do
First run Doctor.
If OpenSSL, Java or keytool is reported missing, run FIX_PATH_AND_CHECK_PWA_FIXED.bat from the toolkit folder.
It searches common installed locations and adds found program folders to your User PATH.
It does not install missing programs.
Reopen Excel and Command Prompt, then rerun the check.
Run Doctor first.
Record the exact OpenSSL, Java and keytool messages.
These are checks, not proof the app itself is broken.
If one says NOT FOUND IN PATH, close Excel and Command Prompt before repair.
Locate FIX_PATH_AND_CHECK_PWA_FIXED.bat in the toolkit folder.
Double-click the repair BAT.
It checks Git OpenSSL and common JDK locations and modifies only your User PATH when it finds an installed program.
It does not install programs.
Follow the numbered stages.
At the optional project-folder question, select your actual website folder or press Enter to skip.
Do not move website files into dist merely to satisfy a check.
Read the finished log at logs\PATH_REPAIR_latest.log beside the repair BAT.
If a command is genuinely missing, use its official installer before repeating the check.
Close and reopen Command Prompt and Excel so they can see updated PATH entries.
In a new Command Prompt run openssl version, java -version, and keytool -help.
Run Doctor again.
Verify the tool lines have changed to PASS; separate website-configuration warnings may remain.

If Java is not installed, download a compatible JDK from its official publisher rather than adding a nonexistent folder.

This appendix defines every technical term used in this book.
Each definition is 2–3 sentences in plain English.
Terms are listed alphabetically.
.aab — Android App Bundle.
The binary file format Google Play accepts for app submission.
It contains your app's compiled code, resources, and signing information.
Google Play uses the .aab to generate optimized .apk files for each device.
Ad Hoc distribution — An Apple distribution method that limits app installation to specific registered devices (up to 100 per year per developer account).
Used for testing on real devices before TestFlight.
We do not use Ad Hoc in this book.
altool — Apple's command-line tool for uploading .ipa files to App Store Connect.
Invoked by the cloud Mac in the iOS workflow YAML ( xcrun altool --upload-app ).
Replaces the older Application Loader tool.
AndroidManifest.xml — The central configuration file of every Android app.
Declares the app's package name, permissions, activities, and minimum Android version.
Capacitor generates this file when you run npx cap add android .
Android Studio — Google's official IDE for Android development, free.
We introduce emulator setup in Chapter 30 for the Android emulator.
Not required for production builds (those happen on cloud Linux via GitHub Actions).
.apk — Android Package.
The binary file format that Android devices install directly.
Google Play generates .apk files from your uploaded .aab , optimized for each device.
App ID — Apple's term for the unique identifier of your app, in reverse-DNS format (e.g., com.example.myapp ).
Same concept as Bundle ID.
Registered in Apple Developer Portal → Identifiers.
App Store Connect — Apple's web portal for managing your apps on the App Store.
Where you submit builds, write store listings, view sales, and respond to reviews.
URL: appstoreconnect.apple.com .
App Store Connect API — Apple's REST API for programmatic access to App Store Connect.
Used by the cloud Mac to upload builds without 2FA.
Authenticated by the .p8 API key.
.cer — A digital certificate file in DER binary format.
Apple issues this file when you upload a CSR.
Bundled with your private key to create a .p12 .
Certificate — A digital document that binds a public key to an identity (your name, your organization).
Apple and Google issue certificates after you prove your identity.
Used to sign app binaries.
CocoaPods — The dependency manager for iOS projects, similar to npm for JavaScript.
Reads a Podfile and downloads native iOS dependencies.
The cloud Mac runs pod install during the iOS build.
com.example.myapp — A placeholder Bundle ID used throughout this book. com.example.* is reserved by IANA and cannot be published to a real store.
Replace with your own unique Bundle ID.
CORS — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing.
A browser security mechanism that blocks JavaScript from reading files loaded via the file:// protocol.
Causes "blank white screen" on iOS WKWebView.
Fixed by setting iosScheme: ionic in capacitor.config.json .
CSR — Certificate Signing Request.
A file you generate from your private key, containing your public key and identity info.
Uploaded to Apple/Google, who use it to issue your distribution certificate.
.der — Distinguished Encoding Rules.
A binary format for storing certificates.
Apple's .cer files use DER.
Convert to PEM with openssl x509 -inform DER -outform PEM .
Developer Portal — Apple's web portal at developer.apple.com/account/resources for managing certificates, identifiers, and profiles.
Where you generate certificates, register App IDs, and download provisioning profiles.
Distribution Certificate — An Apple-issued certificate that allows you to sign apps for App Store distribution.
Distinguished from "Development Certificate" (used for testing only).
.gitignore — A text file in your project root that tells Git which files to exclude from version control.
Critical for preventing signing keys from being committed to a public repo.
GitHub Actions — GitHub's continuous integration service.
Runs commands on virtual machines (Linux, Windows, or macOS) when you push code.
Free for 2,000 minutes/month per personal account.
GitHub Pages — A static site hosting service bundled with GitHub.
Hosts your privacy policy for free at yourusername.github.io/your-repo/ .
GitHub Secrets — Encrypted environment variables stored in your GitHub repo.
Used to pass signing keys, passwords, and API keys to GitHub Actions workflows.
Never visible after saving.
Git Bash — A Linux-style terminal that ships with Git for Windows.
Understands Linux commands like mkdir , cd , ls , cat .
The "black window" used throughout this book.
Gradle — The build system for Android projects.
Reads build.gradle files, compiles your app, and produces .aab or .apk files.
The cloud Linux runs ./gradlew bundleRelease during the Android build.
HTTPS transport backend — An option in the Git for Windows installer.
Choosing "Use the OpenSSL library" installs OpenSSL, which we use to forge Apple signing keys.
.ipa — iPhone Application Archive.
The binary file format Apple's App Store accepts for iOS app submission.
Contains your compiled app, signing information, and provisioning profile.
iPhone — Apple's smartphone line. iOS apps run on iPhone.
Apple also makes iPad (running iPadOS, similar to iOS) and Apple Watch (running watchOS, separate from this book).
IPv6 — Internet Protocol version 6.
The newer internet address format.
Apple requires your app's network connections to work over IPv6.
Most modern web APIs already support IPv6.
Java JDK — Java Development Kit.
Required to run keytool (for generating Android keystores).
We install Adoptium Temurin JDK 17 in Chapter 19.
keytool — A Java command-line tool for generating keystores.
Ships with the Java JDK.
Used in Chapter 18 to create my-release-key.jks .
Keystore — A password-protected file containing cryptographic keys.
Android uses the .jks keystore format to sign app binaries.
LTS — Long Term Support.
A version of Node.js that receives bug fixes and security patches for 30 months.
We install Node.js LTS (currently v22) instead of the "Current" version.
Mac Tax — The informal term for the historical requirement to buy a $1,000+ Mac to compile iOS binaries.
This book bypasses the Mac Tax using GitHub Actions cloud Macs.
manifest.json — A JSON file in your PWA's dist/ folder.
Tells browsers "this is an app, not a webpage".
Declares the app's name, icons, theme color, and start URL.
Node.js — A JavaScript runtime that lets Windows PCs execute JavaScript outside a browser.
Required because the Capacitor tooling ( npm , npx ) is written in JavaScript.
npm — Node Package Manager.
The default package manager for Node.js.
Used to install Capacitor and other JavaScript packages from the npm registry.
npx — Node Package Executor.
Runs a command from a locally-installed npm package without needing to install it globally.
Used to run npx cap init , npx cap sync , etc.
.p12 — PKCS#12 format.
A password-protected archive containing your private key + Apple's certificate.
The cloud Mac uses the .p12 to sign iOS builds.
Same as .pfx .
.p8 — A text file format for storing elliptic curve private keys.
Apple's App Store Connect API uses .p8 keys for headless authentication (no 2FA required).
PATH — An environment variable that lists folders Windows searches when you type a command.
If a program is not in PATH, you get "command not found" errors.
.pem — Privacy-Enhanced Mail.
A text format for storing certificates and keys, base64-encoded between -----BEGIN ...----- and -----END ...----- lines.
OpenSSL tools prefer PEM over DER.
Personal Access Token (PAT) — A 40-character random string GitHub uses instead of your account password for command-line authentication.
Created at github.com/settings/tokens .
Scoped to specific permissions.
Pods — iOS dependencies managed by CocoaPods.
Stored in ios/App/Pods/ .
Excluded from Git via .gitignore .
Privacy Policy — A document describing what data your app collects and how you use it.
Both Apple and Google REQUIRE a hosted privacy policy URL before accepting submissions.
Provisioning Profile — A file from Apple that links your App ID, distribution certificate, and the permission to install on devices.
Stored as .mobileprovision .
Embedded inside the .ipa at build time.
PWA — Progressive Web App.
A website with manifest.json and a service worker ( sw.js ) that behaves like a native app when added to home screen.
The starting point for this book.
RSA — Rivest–Shamir–Adleman.
The asymmetric cryptography algorithm used by Apple and Google for app signing. 2048-bit RSA is the minimum accepted key length.
Service Account — A Google Cloud robot account used for programmatic access.
We create a service account in Chapter 26 to let GitHub Actions upload to Google Play without 2FA.
Service Worker (sw.js) — A JavaScript file that runs in the background in a browser or WebView.
Intercepts network requests, enables offline functionality, and handles push notifications.
Simulator — Apple's iOS Simulator, runs only on macOS.
Lets you test iOS apps on a virtual iPhone.
We cannot use Simulator on Windows; we use TestFlight on real iPhones instead.
TestFlight — Apple's beta testing platform.
Distributes pre-release builds to up to 10,000 testers.
Builds expire after 90 days.
URL: appstoreconnect.apple.com → TestFlight tab.
UAC — User Account Control.
Windows' security feature that prompts "Do you want to allow this app to make changes to your device?" when running installers.
Click YES to proceed.
WebView / WKWebView — A hidden full-screen browser component on Android (WebView) and iOS (WKWebView).
Capacitor wraps your PWA inside a WebView, removing the browser address bar and exposing native bridges.
Windows Key + S — Keyboard shortcut to open Windows Search.
Used to launch Git Bash, VS Code, and other installed programs by name.
Xcode — Apple's official IDE for iOS development, free, runs only on macOS.
The cloud Mac has Xcode pre-installed and uses it to build your .ipa .
YAML — YAML Ain't Markup Language.
A human-readable data format used for GitHub Actions workflow files ( .github/workflows/*.yml ).
Whitespace-sensitive — use 2-space indentation, never tabs.

General & Eligibility
Can I do this on a Mac instead of Windows?
Yes, and the workflow is somewhat simpler — you can run Xcode natively, use Mac Keychain Access for signing keys, and skip the GitHub Actions cloud Mac entirely.

However, you still need this book for: the GitHub Actions YAMLs (optional but recommended for automated builds), the Google Cloud service account setup (Chapter 26), the privacy policy template (Chapter 34), and the 12-tester requirement (Chapter 38).
If you have a Mac, replace the cloud Mac build steps with local xcodebuild commands; everything else applies verbatim.
Can I do this on Linux?
Yes, with caveats.
Node.js, Git, OpenSSL, and VS Code all run natively on Linux.
You can generate the Apple signing keys with OpenSSL exactly as in Chapter 14.
You can install Android Studio for the emulator (Chapter 30).
However, you cannot build iOS binaries locally — Linux cannot run Xcode.
You must use the GitHub Actions cloud Mac (Chapter 24) for iOS builds, exactly as Windows users do.
Use a Linux equivalent of deploy.bat (a .sh script) for the one-click deploy.
Do I need to be a US resident?
No.
Apple Developer Program and Google Play Console accept developers from virtually every country.
Both accept international credit/debit cards for the enrollment fee.
The only restriction: in some countries, Apple and Google require additional tax forms before you can sell paid apps.
For free apps, no tax forms are required.
I am under 18.
Can I publish apps?
Apple: minors (under 18 in most countries) cannot legally enter the Apple Developer Agreement.
A parent or guardian must enroll using their own Apple ID and add the minor as a "User" with appropriate permissions in App Store Connect.
Google: Google accounts can be created at age 13+ (varies by country).
Play Console requires the account holder to be of legal age to contract in their jurisdiction.
For users under 18, a parent should manage the account using Family Link.
Is this workflow legal?
Yes.
All tools used (Node.js, Git, OpenSSL, Capacitor, GitHub Actions) are open-source or officially licensed for this purpose.

Apple's developer agreement does not prohibit using cloud Macs for builds — it only prohibits sharing your signing key with untrusted third parties, which we do not do (GitHub Secrets are encrypted, and the cloud Mac is wiped after each build).
Google's terms similarly allow CI/CD automation.
Cost & Time
What is the total cost to ship one app to both stores?
Apple Developer Program: $99/year, recurring
Google Play Console: $25, one-time
GitHub account: Free (2,000 Actions minutes/month)
All other tools (Node, Git, VS Code, Capacitor, OpenSSL): Free
Year 2+ total: $99/year (only Apple renews)
If you exceed 2,000 GitHub Actions minutes: $0.008/minute for Linux/Windows, $0.08/minute for macOS.
For a hobbyist, this is rare.
How long does the entire process take?
Hands-on time: 8–12 hours, spread across a weekend.

Wall-clock time including waits: 5–10 days, due to: - Apple Developer account verification: 1–5 business days - Google Play identity verification: 1–3 business days - Apple App Store review: 24–48 hours - Google Play review: 3–5 business days - Google 12-tester requirement (if applicable): 14 days continuous
These waits overlap.
Start the Apple and Google account enrollments FIRST (Chapter 11 and Chapter 12), then proceed through Parts IV and V while the accounts verify.
Can I complete the book in a single weekend?
The hands-on work fits in a weekend, but the waits do not.

Realistic plan: - Saturday : Parts I, II, IV (8 hours hands-on) - Sunday : Parts V, VI (4 hours hands-on; cloud builds run in parallel) - Monday–Friday : Wait for Apple/Google account verification, then submit - Following Monday : Stores approve (or request changes)
If you skip ahead without waiting for account verification, you will hit blockers in Part IV.
Can I publish to only one store?
Yes, completely fine.
Many apps ship to only one store first, then expand later.
To skip Apple: ignore Chapters 10, 13–17, 23, 30, 34 and skip the iOS-related Secrets in Chapter 21.
To skip Google: ignore Chapters 11, 18, 24, 25, 31, 35, 37 and skip the Android-related Secrets.
Workflow & Tooling
Can I use a different CI service than GitHub Actions?
Yes — GitLab CI, CircleCI, Travis CI, Bitrise, and Codemagic all offer similar functionality.
Bitrise and Codemagic are specifically designed for mobile CI/CD and include iOS signing helpers.
The trade-off: most alternatives cost money beyond a small free tier.
GitHub Actions' 2,000 included monthly minutes (macOS runners billed at 10×, so ~200 macOS-equivalent minutes) is the most generous free option for hobbyists.
What about Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)?
WSL lets you run a Linux terminal inside Windows, with full access to Linux command-line tools.
It is a valid alternative to Git Bash.
However, this book assumes Git Bash for consistency.
If you prefer WSL: install Node, Git, OpenSSL, and VS Code in WSL (using apt install ); the commands in this book work identically.
WSL does NOT give you a Mac — you still need the GitHub Actions cloud Mac for iOS builds.
Can I do this without GitHub at all?
Yes, but harder.
Alternatives: - Self-hosted Mac mini ($600+ used): run Xcode locally.
Defeats the "zero-Mac" goal. - Cloud Mac rentals (MacStadium, $50+/month): pay monthly for a cloud Mac.
More expensive than GitHub Actions for a hobbyist. - Bitrise/Codemagic ($50+/month): mobile-specific CI services.
Easier than GitHub Actions but cost money.
GitHub's free tier is the best deal for hobbyists publishing one or two apps.
What if I have multiple PWAs?
Each PWA needs its own GitHub repository, its own set of GitHub Secrets, and its own Apple App ID + Google Play app entry.
You CAN reuse the same Apple Distribution Certificate and .p8 API key across multiple apps (one cert can sign many apps; one API key can upload to many apps).
For Android, each app needs its own keystore (do not reuse keystores across apps — if one keystore leaks, only one app is compromised).
Can I edit the YAML workflow files myself?
Yes — they are plain text in .github/workflows/ .
Once you understand the structure (triggers → jobs → steps), you can add custom steps: send a Slack notification on success, run unit tests before building, deploy to multiple TestFlight groups, etc.
The YAML syntax is documented at docs.github.com/actions .
Always test changes by pushing a small commit and watching the workflow run.
What is the difference between TestFlight and App Store?
TestFlight is Apple's beta testing platform — apps distributed via TestFlight are pre-release, marked with an orange dot, and expire after 90 days.
Up to 10,000 testers can install TestFlight builds.
The App Store is the public, permanent distribution channel — apps on the App Store do not expire and are available to anyone with an iPhone.
TestFlight is for testing; App Store is for production.
Account & Security
What happens if I stop paying Apple's $99/year fee?
You have a 30-day grace period after the renewal date.

If you do not pay within 30 days: - Your apps are removed from the App Store (existing users keep the app) - Your certificates are revoked (you cannot push updates or new TestFlight builds) - Your provisioning profiles stop working
If you later re-enroll (within 5 years), your apps and certificates can be restored.
After 5 years, your developer ID is permanently released and cannot be reused.
What happens if Google suspends my account?
Google suspends accounts for serious policy violations (malware, fraud, repeat offenses).
All your apps are immediately removed from Google Play.
Existing users keep the app but cannot receive updates.
The $25 fee is non-refundable.
You can appeal via support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/gethelp , but appeals rarely succeed.

To avoid suspension: read and follow the Developer Program Policies ( play.google.com/console/about/developer-policies ), respond to user data deletion requests within 30 days, and do not submit apps that violate user trust.
Can I transfer ownership of my app to another developer?
Yes, both stores support app transfers.
Apple: App Store Connect → your app → "App Information" → scroll to "Transfer App".
The recipient must have their own Apple Developer account and accept the transfer.
Bundle ID, reviews, and download history transfer with the app.
Google: Play Console → Setup → Advanced Settings → App transfer.
The recipient must have their own Play Console account and accept the transfer.
The recipient's signing key replaces yours.
Transfers are typically used when selling an app business or moving an app from a personal account to a company account.
Can I use the same Apple ID for personal and developer use?
Yes — and you should.
The Apple ID you use for iCloud, App Store purchases, and Apple Music is the same Apple ID you use for developer enrollment.
Do not create a separate developer-only Apple ID; it complicates 2FA and App Store Connect access.
Use ONE Apple ID for everything.
Someone got access to my GitHub repo.
What do I do?
If a malicious collaborator was added to your repo, they may have created a workflow that printed your Secrets to a log they could read.
Treat all Secrets as compromised:
Remove the collaborator from your repo settings immediately.
Revoke your Apple Distribution Certificate on Apple Developer Portal.
Generate a new private key + CSR + .cer + .p12 (Chapters 15–17).
Revoke your App Store Connect API key.
Generate a new one (Chapter 18).
Generate a new Android keystore (Chapter 19) — note: this means Google Play may offer an upload-key reset through approved Play App Signing support.
Generate a new Google Cloud service account (Chapter 26).
Update all GitHub Secrets with new values.
Re-run deploy.bat to push new builds.
This is painful — which is why we emphasized only inviting collaborators you trust.
Signing & Keys
Can I change my app's Bundle ID after publishing?
No, never.
The Bundle ID is permanently embedded in your binary and registered with Apple/Google.
Changing it requires publishing a brand-new app — your existing users would NOT automatically migrate, and you would lose all reviews and download history.
Choose your Bundle ID carefully before Chapter 7.
Use reverse-DNS format: com.yourname.appname .
All lowercase, dots only, no spaces or special chars.
Can I change my app's display name later?
Yes.
The display name (what users see under the icon) can be changed at any time by submitting an update.
Apple re-reviews the new name.
Google accepts name changes without re-review.
Bundle ID stays the same; only the display name changes.
What if I lose my Apple signing key (.key file)?
If you lose ios_distribution.key , you cannot sign new builds with the existing Apple Distribution Certificate.
Recovery: 1.
Revoke the existing certificate on Apple Developer Portal. 2.
Generate a new private key + CSR + .cer + .p12 (Chapters 15–17). 3.
Update BUILD_CERTIFICATE_BASE64 , P12_PASSWORD , and PROVISIONING_PROFILE_BASE64 GitHub Secrets. 4.
Existing TestFlight builds stop working until you upload a new build signed with the new cert. 5.
App Store version stays live — only TestFlight and future updates are affected.
This is annoying but recoverable.
Apple's design allows key rotation without losing your published app.
What if I lose my Android keystore (.jks file)?
Catastrophic.
Google requires every Android update to be signed with the same key as the original release.

If you lose the keystore: - You cannot update the existing app on Google Play. - The only recovery path: contact Google Play support and request a "key upgrade" — a lengthy process requiring identity re-verification. - Alternatively: publish a brand-new app with a different package name.
Your existing users would NOT migrate automatically.
This is why Chapter 18 emphasizes backing up the keystore to a USB stick IMMEDIATELY after generation.
Should I use Google Play App Signing (let Google hold my key)?
For beginners, no — self-managed signing (Chapter 19) is simpler and gives you full control.
Play App Signing is useful for large organizations that want Google to manage key rotation and security.
The trade-off: once you opt in to Play App Signing, you cannot opt out.
And you depend on Google to sign your updates.
If you later want to switch to Play App Signing, you can opt in via Play Console → Setup → App integrity → "Upgrade signing key".
The reverse (going from Play App Signing back to self-managed) is not supported.
Can I reuse my Apple Distribution Certificate across multiple apps?
Yes — and you should.
One Distribution Certificate can sign up to ~50 apps on the same Apple Developer account.
Generate the cert + .p12 once (Chapters 15–17), then create a separate App ID and provisioning profile per app (Chapter 17).
Reuse the same .p12 in each app's GitHub Secrets.
For Android, do NOT reuse the keystore across apps.
Each app gets its own .jks.
If one app's keystore leaks, only that app is compromised.
Store Submission
My app was rejected with "Guideline 4.3 — Spam".
What does this mean?

Apple's most common rejection for new developers. 4.3 means: "Your app is too similar to existing apps, or has limited functionality, or does not provide enough unique value." Common triggers: - A clone of an existing popular app - An app that just wraps a website without adding native features - Multiple similar apps from the same developer (e.g., "Travel App for City X" × 20)
Recovery: add genuinely unique features that differentiate your app from existing alternatives.
Document the unique value in your app description.
Re-submit.
If you genuinely believe the rejection is wrong, appeal via App Store Connect → "Submit an Appeal".
Apple rejected for "Guideline 2.1 — App Completeness".
What now?
2.1 means the reviewer found your app does not function as described, or features are missing, or it crashes during testing.
The rejection email tells you exactly what they tested and what failed.
Recovery: 1.
Reproduce the issue locally (Chapter 27) or via TestFlight (Chapter 31). 2.
Fix the underlying bug. 3.
Re-run deploy.bat to upload a new build. 4.
In App Store Connect, select the new build on the 1.0 page. 5.
Reply to the rejection in Resolution Center explaining what you fixed. 6.
Re-submit.
Apple's reviewers usually re-review within 24 hours of resubmission.
Can I appeal a rejection I think is wrong?
Yes.
In App Store Connect, open the rejection → "Resolution Center" → write a polite, specific reply explaining why you believe the rejection is incorrect.
Reference the exact Guideline they cited and explain how your app complies.
Apple's review team reconsiders within 24–48 hours.
For Google: respond to the policy violation email with your appeal.
Google's response time is 3–7 business days.
How long does Apple's review really take?
For first submissions: typically 24–48 hours, sometimes as fast as 6 hours, occasionally as long as 5 days during high-traffic periods (Christmas, WWDC week, iPhone launch week).
For updates to existing apps: typically 12–24 hours, often faster.
You can track current review times at appreviewtimes.com (community-sourced) or developer.apple.com/app-store/review (Apple's official status page).
How long does Google Play's review take?
For first submissions: typically 3–5 business days.
For updates: typically 1–3 business days.
Google's review is generally less strict than Apple's, but the 12-tester requirement (Chapter 38) adds 14 days for personal accounts created after Nov 13, 2023.
After Publication
How do I update my app after it is published?
Edit your web files in dist/ (fix bugs, add features).

Bump the version number in three places: - package.json : "version": "1.0.1" (was 1.0.0) - ios/App/App/Info.plist : increment CFBundleVersion (e.g., from 1 to 2 ) - android/app/build.gradle : increment versionCode (e.g., from 1 to 2 ) and versionName (e.g., from "1.0.0" to "1.0.1" )
Run deploy.bat .
Type a commit message like "v1.0.1: fix map rendering".
Watch the cloud builds complete (~20 min iOS, ~10 min Android).
In App Store Connect: select the new build on the "1.0.1 Prepare for Submission" page → submit for review.
In Play Console: create a new production release → upload the new .aab → start rollout.
Users get the update automatically (iOS within 24 hours of approval, Android immediately).
Can I remove my app from stores later?
Yes.
Both stores support "unpublishing": - Apple: App Store Connect → your app → "Pricing and Availability" → "Remove from Sale".

Existing users keep the app and can re-download from their purchase history, but no new users can install it. - Google: Play Console → your app → "Setup" → "Advanced Settings" → "App Availability" → "Unpublished".
Same behavior — existing users keep it, no new installs.
You can re-publish later (within 5 years for Apple, indefinitely for Google) without losing reviews or download history.
How do I add push notifications?

Beyond this book's scope, but here is the high-level path: - iOS: register for APNs (Apple Push Notifications service) in your Apple Developer Portal → create a Push Notification certificate (separate from your Distribution cert) → add the @capacitor/push-notifications plugin → request permission from the user → handle incoming notifications in JavaScript. - Android: register for FCM (Firebase Cloud Messaging) → add @capacitor/push-notifications plugin → create a Firebase project → upload the google-services.json to your Android project → request permission → handle notifications.
Budget 2–4 hours to set up push notifications on both platforms.
Capacitor's documentation at capacitorjs.com/docs/apis/push-notifications walks through the integration.
How do I add in-app purchases (IAP)?
Significantly more complex than push notifications.
Required for any digital goods sold inside your app (Apple's 3.1.1 guideline forbids external payment links for digital goods).
iOS path: Apple StoreKit framework → create IAP products in App Store Connect → integrate @capacitor-community/in-app-purchases plugin → handle purchase flows → verify receipts server-side.
Android path: Google Play Billing → create IAP products in Play Console → integrate billing client → handle purchase flows → verify with Google Play Developer API.
Budget 1–2 weeks for a complete IAP implementation with proper receipt validation.
Consider using a service like RevenueCat (free up to $10K monthly revenue) which abstracts both platforms.
Alternative Approaches
Should I use Expo instead of Capacitor?
Expo is a different PWA-to-native framework.
Pros: zero native configuration, OTA updates built-in.
Cons: requires ejecting for many native features, larger binary size, Expo EAS Build (cloud build service) costs money beyond free tier.
If your existing PWA is already built with React Native + Expo, use Expo.
If your PWA is plain HTML/CSS/JS or built with React/Vue/Angular/Svelte, use Capacitor (this book).
Both are valid choices; Capacitor is more flexible for arbitrary PWAs.
Should I rewrite my PWA as a native React Native / Flutter app?
No, unless you have a compelling reason.
Capacitor wraps your existing PWA — no rewrite needed.
If you later want native features Capacitor plugins do not provide (custom camera UI, complex animations, AR/VR), consider rewriting.
But for 95% of apps, the Capacitor wrapper is sufficient and saves months of work.
Can I use this workflow for an Expo or React Native app?
Partially.
The signing key generation (Part IV), GitHub Actions setup (Part V), and store submission (Part VII) chapters apply to any iOS/Android app.
The Capacitor-specific chapters (Part II) do not apply.
Expo users should use Expo EAS Build instead of GitHub Actions for cloud builds.
Privacy & Legal
Do I need a privacy policy if my app collects no data?
Yes, both Apple and Google REQUIRE a privacy policy URL for every app, even if it collects no data.
The policy must declare that the app collects no data and explain what would happen if it ever did.
Use the template in Chapter 33 — modify Section 1 to declare "no data collected" if applicable.
What about GDPR (European Union) and CCPA (California)?

GDPR and CCPA require: - A clear privacy policy (Chapter 34 covers this) - A way for users to request data deletion (your app must include a "Delete my account" feature, or you must respond to deletion emails within 30 days) - Consent for non-essential cookies/tracking (your app should not set tracking cookies without consent) - Data portability (export user data on request)
For PWAs that store data only locally on the device (no server-side storage), GDPR/CCPA compliance is straightforward — uninstalling the app deletes all data.
The Chapter 34 privacy policy template reflects this.
If your app has a backend server storing user data, consult a lawyer to customize the privacy policy and implement proper data subject rights.
Can my app use external APIs (like Google Maps, OpenWeather, etc.)?
Yes, with these considerations: - The API key must NOT be hardcoded in your app's source code — anyone could extract it.

Use a backend proxy server to hide the key, or use a service like Google Maps Platform's per-app restrictions. - Your app's network requests must work over IPv6 (Apple requires this — most modern APIs already do). - CORS: if your PWA calls an external API from JavaScript, the API must allow your app's origin.
Capacitor's ionic://localhost scheme is treated as a web origin. - Rate limits: respect the API provider's rate limits to avoid being banned.
What is the "Mac Tax" you keep mentioning?
The informal term for the historical requirement that iOS developers buy a $1,000+ Mac to compile iPhone binaries.
Apple's official toolchain (Xcode) only runs on macOS, and Xcode is the only signed-binary producer Apple blesses.

This book's entire architecture exists to bypass the Mac Tax: GitHub Actions provides a cloud Mac (2,000 included minutes/month, macOS billed at 10×), OpenSSL on Windows generates the same PKCS#12 signing files Mac Keychain would produce, and Apple's App Store Connect API enables headless uploads without 2FA SMS prompts.
The total cost: $99/year to Apple + $25 one-time to Google + $0 to GitHub.
Troubleshooting Tips
My app crashes for some users but not others.
How do I debug?
This is almost always a device-specific issue.
Steps: 1.
Check App Store Connect → Metrics → Crashes (iOS) and Play Console → Android Vitals → Crashes (Android).
Both show stack traces and affected device models. 2.
Identify the common factor: a specific Android version?
A specific iPhone model?
Low-memory devices? 3.
Try to reproduce locally — sometimes using the Android emulator with a different API level (Chapter 30) reproduces the issue. 4.
If you cannot reproduce, integrate a crash reporting service: Sentry (free tier 5,000 events/month), Bugsnag (7,500/month), or Firebase Crashlytics (free).
These capture stack traces in real-time from real users.
My app was approved but no one can find it in search.
Why?
App Store search ranking depends on: app name, subtitle, keywords field, download velocity, ratings, and reviews.

To improve discoverability: - Use relevant keywords in your app name (e.g., "TravelApp — Discover Local Spots" not just "TravelApp") - Fill all 100 characters of the Keywords field with comma-separated relevant terms - Encourage early users to leave reviews (Apple's API lets you prompt for review after a positive interaction) - Run Apple Search Ads (pay per click) to boost early visibility
Google Play ranking is similar: app name, short description, long description (keyword density matters), and download/engagement metrics.
How do I localize my app for multiple languages?
Both stores support localizing your store listing (screenshots, description, keywords) for any language.

For the app itself: - Use the standard Intl JavaScript API for date/number/currency formatting - Use a translation library (i18next, vue-i18n, react-intl) for UI strings - Detect the user's language via navigator.language and load the appropriate translation file
Apple requires localized screenshots for each language you support.
Google auto-translates your description if you do not provide a translation.
Budget 2–4 hours per language for translation (more if you hire a human translator; less if you use machine translation with human review).

Open a fresh Git Bash. 3.

Cause: Same as node not found — npm ships with Node.

bash: keytool: command not found
Cause: Java JDK is not installed, OR your terminal was open during Java install.
Fix: 1.
Close Git Bash. 2.
Open fresh Git Bash. 3.

If java -version works but keytool fails, restart your PC.

Section 3: Certificate & Signing Errors
Invalid CSR from Apple Developer Portal
Cause: CSR generated with wrong key size, missing field, or invalid -subj .
Fix: 1.
Regenerate private key: openssl genrsa -out ios_distribution.key 2048 2.
Regenerate CSR with correct -subj : /emailAddress=YOUR_EMAIL/CN=YOUR_NAME/C=YOUR_COUNTRY 3.
Re-upload CSR.
No certificate matches private key
Cause: The .pem and .key files do not correspond (you regenerated one without the other).
Fix: 1.
Re-download the .cer from Apple (the one matching your current .key ). 2.
Re-convert to PEM: openssl x509 -in distribution.cer -inform DER -out distribution.pem -outform PEM 3.
Re-bundle: openssl pkcs12 -export -inkey ios_distribution.key -in distribution.pem -out distribution.p12 -passout pass:PASSWORD
Keystore was tampered with, or password was incorrect
Cause: ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD Secret does not match the keystore's actual password.
Fix: 1.
Test locally: keytool -list -v -keystore my-release-key.jks — enter password. 2.
If you forgot the password, regenerate the keystore (Chapter 19) — but if you have already published, you cannot fix this.
xcodebuild: error: No signing certificate "iOS Distribution" found
Cause: The .p12 import into the cloud Mac's keychain failed.
Fix: 1.
Verify BUILD_CERTIFICATE_BASE64 is correct (re-encode if needed). 2.
Verify P12_PASSWORD matches Chapter 15 Step 2. 3.
Test locally: openssl pkcs12 -in distribution.p12 -noout -info — enter password.
If it fails, regenerate.
altool: error: Could not find the keychain entry
Cause: The .p8 API key was not written to the correct file path on the cloud Mac.
Fix: 1.
Verify APP_STORE_CONNECT_KEY_ID (10-char alphanumeric). 2.
Verify APP_STORE_CONNECT_PRIVATE_KEY includes -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY----- and -----END PRIVATE KEY----- lines. 3.
The workflow writes the .p8 to ~/.appstoreconnect/private_keys/AuthKey_<KEY_ID>.p8 — verify the KEY_ID matches.
altool: error: 401 Unauthorized
Cause: One of the three API key Secrets is wrong.
Fix: 1.
Re-check Issuer ID (UUID format with hyphens). 2.
Re-check Key ID (10-char alphanumeric). 3.
Re-check Private Key (entire .p8 contents including BEGIN/END lines).
ITMS-90171: Invalid Bundle Structure (Apple upload error)
Cause: Your app's binary contains files outside the allowed structure.
Fix: Usually caused by a Capacitor plugin that includes files it should not.
Update Capacitor plugins to latest versions: npm update @capacitor/* .
ITMS-90713: Missing Info.plist value (Apple upload error)
Cause: Your app's Info.plist is missing a required key.
Fix: The error names the missing key.
Add it to ios/App/App/Info.plist .
ITMS-90809: Deprecated API Usage (Apple upload error)
Cause: Your app uses an iOS API that Apple has deprecated.

Cause: File not at .github/workflows/*.yml , OR default branch is not main .
Fix: 1.
Verify file path: ls .github/workflows/ 2.
Verify default branch in GitHub repo Settings. 3.
If branch is master , change YAML to branches: [ master ] .
macos-14 runner unavailable
Cause: High demand for macOS runners.
Fix: Wait 5–15 minutes.
Try macos-13 as fallback.
Actions billing limit reached
Cause: You exceeded 2,000 free monthly minutes.
Fix: 1.
Wait until next month (quota resets). 2.
Or enable paid Actions: GitHub → Settings → Billing → Actions → set spending limit > $0.
Section 8: Store Submission Errors
Apple Build cannot be selected in App Store Connect
Cause: TestFlight build still processing, or build failed Apple's validation.
Fix: 1.
Check TestFlight tab — wait for "Available for testing" (green dot). 2.
If failed validation, click the build → see rejection reason. 3.
Fix issue, re-run deploy.bat.
Apple Rejection 2.1 - App Completeness
Cause: App does not function as described, or features missing.
Fix: Read rejection email.
Reproduce issue.
Fix code.
Re-run deploy.bat.
Resubmit.
Apple Rejection 5.1.1 - Privacy
Cause: App collects data not declared in App Privacy, or no privacy policy URL.
Fix: Complete Chapter 34 (privacy policy).
Complete App Privacy declaration.
Resubmit.
Google Play Production rollout locked
Cause: 12-tester requirement not satisfied.
Fix: Complete Chapter 38.
Wait 14 days.
Retry.
Google Play Upload rejected - wrong signature
Cause: .aab signed with different keystore than previous uploads.
Fix: Use the original keystore.
